1	Large Language Models (LLMs) with Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning can self-jailbreak: their extended reasoning traces sometimes transition from safe deliberation to committed generation of harmful content. Detecting the precise moment of this safety commitment is essential for real-time intervention, yet no prior work has systematically compared hidden-state (HS) probes against text-based monitors for this task under controlled conditions. We present the first cross-model evaluation of temporal probing methods for safety commitment detection. Our study spans three reasoning models (DeepSeek-R1 8B/32B, QwQ-32B) across two architectures and two scales, and compares HS probes, text monitors, temporal windowing, Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU) sequence models, and geometric baselines including Mahalanobis distance, Bayesian Online Change Point Detection, and Cumulative Sum (CUSUM). Our results reveal three findings. First, temporal context is the dominant factor: expanding the observation window from 1 to 25 reasoning steps improves precision by 12.9 percentage points and reduces false positive rate (FPR) across all models and modalities. Second, the modality advantage is model-dependent: on R1-8B, HS probes Pareto-dominate text probes (+22.4pp precision, $p{<}0.001$; +8.2pp accuracy, $p{=}0.005$; both surviving Bonferroni correction), while on 32B models the advantage is model-dependent, ranging from directional (R1-32B, $p{=}0.080$ uncorrected) to absent (QwQ-32B), with no result surviving Bonferroni correction. Third, geometric change-point methods and cross-model transfer uniformly fail, and these negative results define clear boundaries of current approaches. Control tasks confirm that probes capture genuine safety-relevant structure rather than superficial distributional shifts.

1	Large Language Models (LLMs) with Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning can self-jailbreak: their extended reasoning traces sometimes transition from safe deliberation to committed generation of harmful content. Detecting the precise moment of this safety commitment is essential for real-time intervention, yet no prior work has systematically compared hidden-state (HS) probes against text-based monitors for this task under controlled conditions. We present the first cross-model evaluation of temporal probing methods for safety commitment detection. Our study spans three reasoning models (DeepSeek-R1 8B/32B, QwQ-32B) across two architectures and two scales, and compares HS probes, text monitors, temporal windowing, Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU) sequence models, and geometric baselines including Mahalanobis distance, Bayesian Online Change Point Detection, and Cumulative Sum (CUSUM). Our results reveal three findings. First, temporal context is the dominant factor: expanding the observation window from 1 to 25 reasoning steps improves precision by 12.9 percentage points and reduces false positive rate (FPR) across all models and modalities. Second, the modality advantage is model-dependent: on R1-8B, HS probes Pareto-dominate text probes (+22.4pp precision, $p{<}0.001$; +8.2pp accuracy, $p{=}0.005$; both surviving Bonferroni correction), while on 32B models the advantage is model-dependent, ranging from directional (R1-32B, $p{=}0.080$ uncorrected) to absent (QwQ-32B), with no result surviving Bonferroni correction. Third, geometric distance methods and cross-model transfer fail entirely, and change-point methods (BOCPD, CUSUM) do not improve early detection despite high coverage, defining clear boundaries of current approaches. Control tasks confirm that probes capture genuine safety-relevant structure rather than superficial distributional shifts.

\subsection{Detection Timing Profiles}
\label{sec:timing}

Beyond aggregate accuracy, we examine when probes first detect unsafe reasoning relative to the commitment point (the step at which the model irreversibly begins generating harmful content).

On R1-8B, the HS temporal probe detects unsafe traces at approximately the commitment point itself (lead $\approx$ 0 steps, low FPR). The text temporal probe detects roughly 10 steps earlier (lead $\approx$ +10), but at the cost of higher FPR. This timing asymmetry reflects the nature of the two signals: text features become discriminative as soon as the model begins articulating a plan, while hidden state features consolidate only when the internal representation fully commits to the unsafe trajectory.

This timing trade-off is specific to R1-8B. On QwQ-32B and R1-32B, both modalities show comparable detection timing with no reliable FPR difference between them. We caution against interpreting the R1-8B pattern as a universal property of the two modalities.

\subsection{GRU Sequence Models}
\label{sec:gru}

Static and windowed probes discard sequential structure. We train Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU) classifiers on the full step sequence to ask whether temporal dependencies beyond a fixed window improve early detection. \cref{tab:gru_results} reports crossing accuracy (the accuracy at which the probe first exceeds chance with sustained performance) and detection lead (steps before the commitment point).

\toprule

\caption{GRU sequence model results. Crossing accuracy is the threshold at which sustained above-chance detection begins. Lead is mean steps before commitment point. Multi-layer uses 7 concatenated layers; results are mean$\pm$std over 3 seeds (R1-8B multi only).}
\label{tab:gru_results}

For R1-8B, a single-layer GRU trained on layer 14 hidden states achieves 83.9\% peak accuracy with a crossing point at 72.1\% and a mean lead of +3.5 steps across three seeds. A multi-layer GRU using seven layers reaches 72.9$\pm$4.0\% crossing accuracy with 81.8$\pm$1.0\% peak accuracy, a pre-commitment FPR of 16.5$\pm$4.1\%, and extends the lead to +4.5$\pm$3.0 steps. The worst individual seed achieves a lead of only +0.9 steps, indicating high variance in early detection on this model.

QwQ-32B benefits more from sequence modeling. The single-layer GRU achieves 75.0\% crossing accuracy with a lead of +19.3 steps; the multi-layer variant reaches 84.0\% crossing with +15.9 steps lead. These longer leads suggest that QwQ-32B's hidden states encode planning information well before the commitment point.

R1-32B shows weaker GRU performance overall: single-layer crossing at 30.0\% with +9.1 lead, multi-layer at 23.0\% with +8.8 lead. The low crossing accuracy indicates that R1-32B's safety-relevant signal is more diffuse across layers and harder to capture with a compact sequence model.

All results are reported as mean $\pm$ standard deviation over three random seeds.
